These probabilities come from my general knowledge of NAS-Bench-201, not from looking anything up. The main patterns I relied on:

- Edge 5 (node 2 to 3) and edge 3 (node 0 to 3) both feed the output. When edge 3 is none, the output depends more on the other paths, so edits to edge 5 matter more.
- Edge 0 is the only way into node 1, so when it is none, edges 2 and 4 are effectively dead. Edits to edge 5 then matter differently, because edge 1 is the only remaining route into node 2.
- Most pairs show weak or inconsistent interactions across the three datasets, so N dominates.
